reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard immunology references
clinicalPearls: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder classically presenting in boys with the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections
It is caused by mutations in the WAS gene encoding the WAS protein, which regulates the actin cytoskeleton in haematopoietic cells
The thrombocytopenia is distinctive for producing microthrombocytes (abnormally small platelets), unlike most other causes of low platelets
Bleeding, ranging from petechiae and bruising to serious intracranial haemorrhage, is often the earliest and most dangerous manifestation
The infection pattern reflects combined humoral and cellular immunodeficiency, with encapsulated bacteria, opportunistic organisms, and viruses all contributing
There is a marked predisposition to autoimmune disease (such as haemolytic anaemia and vasculitis) and to malignancy, particularly lymphoma
Milder allelic conditions include X-linked thrombocytopenia, while certain mutations cause X-linked neutropenia

Definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with gene therapy an emerging option; supportive care includes immunoglobulin replacement, infection prophylaxis, and careful bleeding management
reference.pathophysiology: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the WAS gene on the X chromosome, which encodes a protein that links cell-surface signalling to reorganisation of the actin cytoskeleton in blood cells. Defective cytoskeletal dynamics impair the formation of immune synapses, the motility and function of T cells, dendritic cells, and phagocytes, and the normal production and structure of platelets, yielding small, poorly functioning platelets and combined immunodeficiency. Disturbed regulatory T-cell function and abnormal B-cell responses drive the high rate of autoimmunity, while impaired immune surveillance and chronic immune dysregulation predispose to lymphoid malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Severe combined immunodeficiency and other combined immunodeficiencies
Congenital thrombocytopenias with normal platelet size
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film assessing platelet number and platelet size (mean platelet volume)
WAS gene sequencing and analysis of WAS protein expression
Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets and functional T-cell testing
Autoimmune and haemolysis screens where indicated
Surveillance for lymphoma in older patients
redFlags: Significant bleeding, especially intracranial haemorrhage, as an emergency
Recurrent or opportunistic infections requiring urgent immunological workup
New lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms suggesting lymphoma
Live vaccines must be avoided because of the combined immunodeficiency
Blood products should be irradiated and leucodepleted to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease
reference.prognosis: Untreated classic disease carries a poor prognosis owing to bleeding, infection, autoimmunity, and malignancy, but successful haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally performed early, can be curative; milder phenotypes such as X-linked thrombocytopenia have a better outlook though still require monitoring.
pitfalls: Diagnosing isolated ITP and giving immunosuppression or splenectomy without recognising the underlying syndrome
Overlooking the diagnostic clue of small platelet size on the blood film
Administering live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products
Underestimating the lifelong risks of autoimmunity and malignancy after immune reconstitution
Delaying referral for transplantation in a child with classic severe disease
management: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive curative treatment and is best undertaken early, with gene therapy an emerging alternative
Immunoglobulin replacement together with antimicrobial prophylaxis against encapsulated bacteria and Pneumocystis to reduce the combined immunodeficiency infection burden

Bleeding management with platelet support for serious haemorrhage, using irradiated CMV-safe blood products and avoiding antiplatelet agents; splenectomy is generally avoided where transplantation is planned
Eczema care with emollients and topical corticosteroids, and immunosuppression for autoimmune complications such as haemolytic anaemia and vasculitis
Avoidance of live vaccines given the immunodeficiency
Surveillance for lymphoma and other malignancy, particularly in older patients
Genetic counselling for this X-linked disorder with maternal carrier testing and family screening, coordinated through a clinical immunology multidisciplinary team
